offence_severity: 7 years R.I. with fine of Rs.10,000/- and in default of payment of fine, further six months R.I. under Section 376 IPC and four years R.I. with fine of Rs.5,000/- and in default of payment of fine, further three months R.I. under Section 506 IPC
physical_harm: Mild mental retardation and inability to understand the good and bad aspect of sexual assault
number_of_offences: Charged under Sections 376 and 506 IPC; upheld under Sections 376 and 506 IPC
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the medical evidence that the prosecutrix had mild mental retardation with an IQ of 62, which made her unable to understand the good and bad aspect of sexual assault.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses, including the doctors (PW11 and PW22), as credible in establishing the mental retardation of the prosecutrix and the accused's exploitation of her condition.
trial_duration: FIR lodged on 1.4.2008, trial judgment on 14.09.2016, High Court decision on 14.09.2016, Supreme Court decision on 03.12.2020
legal_representation: Ms. Radhika Gautam, Sarthak Ghonkrokta, Aslam, Advs. for the appearing parties
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the prosecutrix was mentally retarded with an IQ of 62, making her unable to understand the nature and consequences of sexual assault. The accused took advantage of her mental illness and low IQ, and he is the biological father of the child delivered by her. The High Court correctly convicted the accused for the offences under Sections 376 and 506 IPC.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the High Court erred in reversing the acquittal, as the trial court's reasoning was plausible. They submitted that there was a delay in lodging the FIR, the prosecutrix's statements were contradictory, and the medical evidence was inconsistent. The accused had already served four years of the seven-year sentence and should not be subjected to further punishment.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that if a victim is unable to understand the nature and consequences of sexual intercourse due to mental illness or unsoundness of mind, the act constitutes rape under Section 375 IPC. The High Court was justified in re-appreciating the evidence and reversing the acquittal.
precedent_relied_upon: Babu v. State of Kerala (2010) 9 SCC 189; Kuldeep Singh v. Commissioner of Police (1999) 2 SCC 10; Vijay Mohan Singh v. State of Karnataka (2019) 5 SCC 436; Krishna v. State of Karnataka (2014) 15 SCC 596
sentencing_rationale: The accused was sentenced to seven years R.I. with a fine of Rs.10,000/- and, in default, further six months R.I. under Section 376 IPC, and four years R.I. with a fine of Rs.5,000/- and, in default, further three months R.I. under Section 506 IPC. The High Court considered the accused's exploitation of the victim's mental illness and the need for a lenient sentence given the circumstances.
judicial_mitigating_factors: The High Court considered the accused's exploitation of the victim's mental illness, his status as the biological father of the child, and the need for special care and affection for individuals with mental disorders.
judicial_aggravating_factors: The High Court considered the accused's false denial of the sexual assault, his taking advantage of the victim's mental illness, and the fact that the victim was unable to understand the nature and consequences of the sexual assault.
other_sentence_order: The accused was sentenced to seven years R.I. with a fine of Rs.10,000/- and, in default, further six months R.I. under Section 376 IPC, and four years R.I. with a fine of Rs.5,000/- and, in default, further three months R.I. under Section 506 IPC.
